steps.step: Read the question – extract the ‘givens’, decide the tools
steps.script:
[S1] Welcome! On this very first slide you can see the whole market puzzle laid out.
[S2] I spot a colourful list: demand, revenue, elasticity, supply… looks busy!
[S1] Exactly. Before we solve anything, let's gather the gifts the examiner already handed us—our “givens.”
[S2] I like free gifts. First one: the demand curve sitting in the top-left corner.
[S1] Yes—notice it links quantity q to price p through that four plus p squared denominator.
[S2] Got it. Next, the bullet that says revenue equals p times q.
[S1] Perfect. Revenue will let us talk about money flows later.
[S2] There’s also a price jump from one to one point one. Seems tiny but important.
[S1] Right—think of it as a gentle tap on the price knob. We’ll use differentials to predict the ripple in revenue.
[S2] I also read “inverse supply equals alpha q plus beta.” Two mysterious symbols to uncover!
[S1] They won’t stay mysterious for long. The equilibrium point—two comma four—gives us one equation, while the producer surplus of two gives us another.
[S2] So two unknowns, two equations—straight-line algebra territory.
[S1] Exactly. Tool-wise, our backpack needs differentiation, elasticity formula, linear approximation, and a pinch of definite integration for surplus.
[S2] All stuff from first-year calculus and intro micro-economics. Phew, within reach.
[S1] Great job summarising. Any anxieties before we dive?
[S2] Just eager to see how elasticity can never break the ceiling of two. Sounds like a magic trick.
[S1] Then let’s roll up our sleeves. On the next slide we’ll take the demand curve apart with the chain rule. Ready?
[S2] Ready and curious!

steps.step: Differentiate the demand curve and build the elasticity formula
steps.script:
[S1] Now, eyes on the demand expression highlighted in blue.
[S2] I see the price buried inside that four plus p squared denominator.
[S1] Question: how would you start finding dq divided by dp?
[S2] Rewrite q as ten times that denominator to the power negative one, then apply the chain rule.
[S1] Superb. Give it a shot—what’s the derivative sign wise?
[S2] The negative pops out, and I get something like minus twenty p over the denominator squared.
[S1] Exactly—great algebraic footwork.
[S2] Next comes elasticity. Formula says E equals negative dq divided by dp times p divided by q.
[S1] Correct. Plug in your derivative and the original q. Notice one power of the denominator cancels—like peeling an onion layer.
[S2] Oh, neat! The dust settles to two p squared over four plus p squared.
[S1] Spot on. That’s our clean elasticity function.
[S2] Feels satisfying to see the clutter disappear.
[S1] And that cancellation trick will keep life simple in the following slide.
[S2] So we’re armed with E of p. What’s next?
[S1] We’ll test whether this expression can ever climb beyond two. Onward!

steps.step: Show that the elasticity never exceeds 2
steps.script:
[S1] Look at the tidy formula we boxed in the top-right: two p squared divided by four plus p squared.
[S2] The numerator looks like a little sibling to the denominator—same p squared but without the four.
[S1] Brilliant observation. For any non-negative p, is p squared smaller than four plus p squared?
[S2] Absolutely—because you’re adding four in the denominator.
[S1] Therefore, the fraction p squared over four plus p squared is always less than one, yet never negative.
[S2] Multiply by two and I see elasticity lives between zero and two.
[S1] Exactly—so our demand never reaches unit trouble beyond two.
[S2] Meaning the curve is relatively inelastic compared with, say, luxury-goods examples.
[S1] That’s a nice economic interpretation.
[S2] Wow, the “never exceed two” claim was just a direct comparison, no extra calculus!
[S1] Sometimes math rewards keen eyesight over brute force. Great job.
[S2] Feeling confident. Let’s put this elasticity badge in our pocket.
[S1] Next stop: building the revenue mountain and finding its peak.

steps.step: Construct the revenue function and locate its turning point
steps.script:
[S1] Shift your gaze to the green box labelled revenue R of p.
[S2] It’s ten p divided by four plus p squared—smooth.
[S1] We need the slope, dR divided by dp. Think quotient rule or product rule-with-negative-power—dealer’s choice.
[S2] I’ll go negative-power again: derivative of p is one, derivative of the denominator piece adds the minus sign…*
[S1] Keep going.
[S2] I end up with ten over four plus p squared minus twenty p squared over the denominator squared.
[S1] Excellent. Combine them under a common denominator.
[S2] Factor ten and I get ten times four minus p squared all over the denominator squared.
[S1] Perfect. Now, what sign does four minus p squared take?
[S2] Positive when p is less than two, zero at p equals two, negative after two.
[S1] Translate that into revenue talk.
[S2] Revenue climbs while price is below two and tumbles once price climbs above two.
[S1] Beautiful economic story: there’s a sweet-spot price of two where revenue tops out.
[S2] Like hiking a hill—up until the summit at two, then down the other side.
[S1] Exactly. Summit reached. Ready for a small price step analysis?
[S2] Bring on the tiny hike from one to one point one!

steps.step: Approximate the revenue change when price rises 1 → 1.1
steps.script:
[S1] Zoom into the red rectangle—linear approximation toolbox.
[S2] The plan: delta R is roughly derivative at one times delta p.
[S1] Spot on. What’s delta p here?
[S2] One tenth—zero point one.
[S1] Earlier we had the derivative formula: ten times four minus p squared over the denominator squared. Plug p equals one.
[S2] Numerator gives thirty, denominator becomes twenty-five, so derivative is one point two.
[S1] Nice arithmetic. Multiply by delta p.
[S2] One point two times zero point one equals zero point one two.
[S1] Meaning revenue should rise by about twelve pence per unit timeframe.
[S2] So a gentle uphill nudge, matching the earlier “revenue increasing for p less than two” insight.
[S1] Exactly—consistency check passed.
[S2] Linear approximation really is a handy pocket lens.
[S1] And you wielded it well. Final leg: cracking the supply curve parameters.

steps.step: Impose the equilibrium and producer-surplus conditions on supply
steps.script:
[S1] Front and centre is the orange supply line: p superscript S equals alpha q plus beta.
[S2] We know the market rests at two units, four currency units price. Plugging those should tie alpha and beta together.
[S1] Right—substituting gives our first equation: two alpha plus beta equals four.
[S2] Noted. Now for the producer surplus clue.
[S1] Surplus is the triangular-looking area between the supply curve and the horizontal price at four, from zero to two units.
[S2] So integrate four minus the supply price with respect to q over zero to two.
[S1] Exactly. Performing that integration leaves a tidy expression: two times four minus beta minus two alpha.
[S2] Setting that equal to two gives four minus beta minus alpha equals one.
[S1] Great. Line them up: Equation one—two alpha plus beta equals four. Equation two—alpha plus beta equals three.
[S2] Subtract to solve: alpha equals one.
[S1] Substitute back and beta becomes two.
[S2] Therefore the inverse supply curve is p superscript S equals q plus two.
[S1] Well done! You transformed abstract symbols into a concrete line.
[S2] Feels like finishing a puzzle—every piece snug.
[S1] Celebrate this victory. We’ve threaded calculus, algebra, and economics into one coherent story.
[S2] Thanks for the guidance. Time to share this newfound knowledge with my study group!
